name: Collagen peptides
lead: Collagen peptides, also called hydrolysed collagen or collagen hydrolysate, are short chains of amino acids produced by enzymatically breaking down animal collagen, usually from bovine, porcine or marine sources. They are sold as powders, drinks and capsules for skin, hair, nails, joints and bone. Collagen itself is a family of structural proteins that make up much of the extracellular matrix of connective tissue, rich in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline [1][2].

The best-studied appearance claim concerns skin. Several randomised trials of oral collagen peptides report improvements in skin hydration, elasticity or wrinkles [3][4][5][6][7], and early systematic reviews described largely consistent benefit [8]. A 2026 meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials of oral and topical peptides found significant improvement in hydration and brightness and a modest pooled effect on wrinkles, with inconsistent effects on elasticity and density [9]. A 2025 meta-analysis in the American Journal of Medicine is reported to have found that skin benefits shrink or vanish in higher-quality and non-industry-funded trials [10].
No sources reviewed here report a hair-growth effect from collagen peptides, though they are frequently marketed for hair.

paras: Marketed as nutricosmetics for skin ageing, hair and nails, collagen peptides are among the most commonly sold beauty supplements [11]. They are often combined with vitamin C, zinc or biotin, as in a drinkable product tested in 72 women aged 35 and older [5].

Collagen peptides have also been investigated for bone mineral density in postmenopausal women [12], muscle recovery and fatigue [13], and in reviews of muscle hypertrophy supplements [14]. Marine collagen has been reviewed as a biomaterial for wound healing, skin anti-ageing and bone regeneration [15].

Skin: a 2020 mechanistic systematic review of 10 publications concluded that oral intact or hydrolysed collagen improved clinical skin-health measures and described three proposed mechanisms [8]. A 2014 randomised trial of specific bioactive collagen peptides reported reduced skin wrinkles and increased dermal matrix synthesis [7], and a 2015 report combined an ex vivo model and trials on skin moisture and the dermal collagen network [4]. Randomised trials of low-molecular-weight collagen peptides reported skin benefits in 2024 and 2025 [3][6].

Meta-analyses: a 2023 meta-analysis of oral collagen for skin anti-ageing and another of hydrolysed collagen for skin rejuvenation are available [16][17]. The 2026 meta-analysis of 19 trials with 1,341 participants reported significant improvement in hydration and brightness, modest wrinkle reduction (mean difference 0.27, p = 0.04), driven by oral polypeptides, and inconsistent elasticity and density effects, with minimal adverse events [9]. The 2025 American Journal of Medicine meta-analysis is described as finding attenuated benefit in higher-quality, non-industry-funded trials [10]. Many individual trials are funded by the manufacturers of the tested products.
Hair: no randomised trial of collagen peptides alone for hair growth was identified in the sources reviewed.

Other outcomes: a randomised trial reported effects on bone mineral density and bone markers in postmenopausal women [12], and registered trials examine bioavailability, skin health and plantar fasciitis [18][19][20].

After digestion, collagen peptides, particularly hydroxyproline-containing di- and tripeptides, are absorbed. The 2020 mechanistic review described direct effects of the peptides on fibroblasts, effects on macrophages and other pathways [8]. An alternative view is that they simply supply amino acids that the body uses like other protein. Bioavailability studies of marine and bovine peptides are registered [18][19]. Research on collagen's role in inflammation and on synthetic collagen-mimetic peptides is ongoing [21][22].
Trials report few adverse events [9]. Possible allergy to marine or bovine sources and contamination in lightly regulated supplements are general considerations discussed for nutricosmetics [11][15].

lore.intro: Collagen peptides are discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a skin and anti-aging supplement, including very high daily doses, and on T Nation as a protein or connective-tissue add-on to training diets [23][24][25].

claims.claim: Mega-dosing collagen peptides (100-140 g a day) visibly improves skin
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports taking about 130 g of collagen daily, says he noticed a difference in his skin and looked younger, and attributes this to higher intake raising the amount that reaches the skin to stimulate collagen and elastin [23].
claims.experts: Randomised trials of oral collagen peptides have used much smaller daily amounts and reported improvements in skin hydration, elasticity or wrinkles, while a 2025 meta-analysis is reported to have found smaller effects in higher-quality and non-industry-funded trials [4][5][7][10]. The thread's poster states that no studies of 100 g or more daily had been done, and no source reviewed here tested such doses [23].

claims.claim: Collagen supplements are a 'cope' for skin
claims.believers: In replies to the mega-dosing thread, one user says he had thought collagen supplements were "cope", while the poster says the cost is comparable to whey and another asks whether collagen shakes should replace whey [23].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of randomised trials report improved skin hydration and a modest effect on wrinkles, with inconsistent effects on elasticity and density, and a 2025 meta-analysis is reported to describe shrinking benefit in higher-quality trials [9][10][16][17].

claims.claim: Collagen peptides taken with vitamin C support tendons and connective tissue
claims.believers: A T Nation member describes trying collagen peptides again with vitamin C (20 g with 1000 mg), spacing the drink 45 minutes before loaded isometric tendon work in his training log [24].
claims.experts: The sources reviewed here describe collagen peptides in bone-density and muscle-damage-recovery research [12][13]; no source reviewed here reports a tendon-specific trial.

claims.claim: Collagen peptides are a cheaper substitute for bone broth
claims.believers: A T Nation reply to a lifter's post asks whether he has thought of replacing bone broth with collagen peptides, saying they would be a lot cheaper and that he uses ones made from beef, fish and eggs [25].
claims.experts: Reviews describe collagen peptides as enzymatically hydrolysed animal collagen sold as powders and drinks, and bioavailability trials have measured peptide absorption from such products; the sources reviewed here do not compare them with bone broth [1][18][19].
